descripcion: At A2 you use a/an and the correctly, plus the simple quantifiers some and any. These small words are used constantly and are often skipped by Spanish speakers. Non-defining clauses and finer quantifiers like much/many come at higher levels.

filas: I have some money. Do you have any?

ejemplos.texto: I have a car and a bike.

notas: The is used when both speaker and listener know which thing is meant.
Some is used in positive sentences, any in questions and negatives.
General nouns often need no article at all: I like music.

contraste.es: Spanish uses articles more widely, even with general nouns (me gusta la música), where English leaves them out (I like music).
contraste.de: German leaves out the article before jobs (Ich bin Lehrerin), which leads to I am teacher instead of I am a teacher. Some and any have no direct German equivalent; German often uses no word at all (Hast du Milch? – Have you got any milk?).
contraste.it: Italian uses the article with general nouns (mi piace la musica) and leaves it out before jobs (sono insegnante), which leads to I like the music and I am teacher. The Italian partitive (del pane) is a good bridge to some (some bread).
contraste.fr: The French partitive is a good bridge: du pain corresponds to some bread, and pas de pain to not any bread. French uses the article with general nouns (j'aime la musique) and leaves it out before jobs (je suis professeur), which leads to I like the music and I am teacher.
contraste.pt: Portuguese uses the article with general nouns (gosto da música) and leaves it out before jobs (sou professor), which leads to I like the music and I am teacher. Some and any have no direct Portuguese equivalent and often need to be added in English.

errores: Adding the before a general noun.
Using any in a positive sentence instead of some.
autochequeo: Have I avoided the before general nouns?
Is some used in positive sentences and any in questions/negatives?
